prime.problem: The bigram lecture builds the same model twice, first by counting and then by training a neural net, over nearly two hours of small tensor steps. Without a map of the few ideas underneath, it is easy to finish with two working scripts and no sense of why they agree, or why the slower one is the one the series keeps.
prime.fits: This card spans the whole course. It compresses the ten bigram cards into six claims, and it leans on micrograd's training loop (forward, zero_grad, backward, update) and the toolkit's softmax and cross-entropy.
expect: sampling one character at a time
shapes and broadcasting deciding the math
the average negative log likelihood as the one score
one-hot @ W plus softmax as the same table, found by gradient descent
prime.goal: Draw the whole bigram pipeline from memory, both routes (count and normalise, or train W by gradient descent), with the loss numbers that show they meet, and say which parts every later model in the series keeps.

attend: Across the whole lecture, which object plays the role of "the model" in the counting route, and which plays it in the neural route?
Which of the six ideas are about what the model is, and which are about how you check that it is right?
Where in the pipeline can a bug run without raising any error, and what number would give it away?
Why does the neural route start with a loss worse than blind guessing, and what does the loss scale let you conclude from that?
If both routes land on the same table, what exactly does the lecture gain by building the second one?

must: A name is len + 1 next-character predictions → counting every pair into a 27×27 table N and dividing each row by its total gives the probabilities that maximise the likelihood → counting is training for a bigram (2.4540 average NLL)

A row of P is a distribution over the next character → draw from it, feed the draw back as the new row, stop at '.' → the model generates names; since it only sees the last character, the names are name-ish but bad (117 one-letter names in 1,000)

The average NLL grades any model with one number (0 perfect, log 27 = 3.2958 uniform) → a zero probability makes it infinite → fake counts (N + 1) keep every probability above 0 at a small cost in training loss (2.4540 → 2.4546)

one-hot @ W picks row W[ix] → exp and normalise (softmax) turn it into probabilities, so W plays log N → gradient descent on the NLL moves W toward log N (3.7590 → 2.4729 in 100 steps) → the net reaches the counting answer from above, and L2 on W plays the fake-count knob
elevated: The counting table needs a row per possible context (27ᵏ rows for k characters: 19,683 for 3) → most rows stay empty → the neural route keeps the same loss, backward and update and only changes how the logits are computed → that is why the series keeps it despite being slower here

P.sum(1) without keepdim has shape (27,), read as a row → on a square table it broadcasts without error and divides columns (row 0 sums to 7.0225) → shape bugs in tensor code fail silently, so shapes must be checked, not trusted
reference: seed 2147483647 and the torch 2.14 samples (cexze., …), which differ from the video's
PyTorch spellings: torch.multinomial(..., replacement=True), F.one_hot(xs, num_classes=27).float(), probs[torch.arange(n), ys], W.grad = None

compress.prompt: Card closed, one sheet of paper: draw the course's whole pipeline from memory, both routes. Top: names → '.'-padded pairs → N → P (with the keepdim that makes rows sum to 1) → the sampling loop. Middle: the loss, with its scale. Bottom: xs → one-hot → @ W → exp → normalise → NLL → backward → update, looping. Draw the arrow that shows both routes meet, and label each part with the big idea it shows.
checklist: 'emma' → .e em mm ma a.; 32,033 names → 228,146 pairs; N is 27 × 27 with row = current char, column = next
P = N / N.sum(1, keepdim=True); without keepdim the columns get divided and row 0 sums to 7.0225
the sampling loop starts at '.' and stops when '.' is drawn
the loss scale: 0 perfect, 2.4540 counting, 3.2958 uniform, ∞ for a zero-count pair, fixed by N + 1 (2.4546)
one-hot @ W = W[ix] = logits, read as log-counts; exp and normalise = softmax
the loop 3.7590 → 2.4729 in 100 steps, approaching 2.4540 from above; 0.01 · mean(W²) plays the fake-count role

retrieve.q: Explain, without code, why normalising the count table and training the one-layer net end at the same loss, and why neither can go below 2.4540 on the training names.
answer: both models see only the previous character, so both are a 27-row table of next-character probabilities
the row-normalised counts are exactly the table that maximises the likelihood of the training bigrams
gradient descent minimises the same NLL, so it can only approach that optimum (2.4729 at 100 steps, 2.4624 at 200)

retrieve.q: Walk one example, the bigram .e, through the neural route: from the index 0 to the number it adds to the loss, naming each tensor and its shape.
answer: xs = 0 → F.one_hot(..., num_classes=27).float() gives a (27,) row with a 1 in slot 0
@ W (27×27) gives the logits, which are just row W[0]
exp gives 27 positive counts; dividing by their sum gives probs that sum to 1
the loss term is −log probs[5] (e = 5); with the random W that is 4.3993

retrieve.q: Fake counts and L2 regularisation both trade training loss for something. What do they buy, what do they cost, and why can't the training loss tell you how much to use?
answer: buy: no probability is ever 0, so unseen pairs get a finite loss ('andrejq' 3.4834 instead of ∞)
cost: the training loss rises (2.4540 → 2.4546 at +1; the regularised net 2.4901 vs 2.4729 at step 99)
the training loss always prefers no smoothing, so the strength must be chosen on held-out names (a dev split, as in exercise E03)

retrieve.q: Counting is exact, instant and has no learning rate. When would you still choose the neural route, and when is counting the better tool?
answer: count when the model really is one character of context: it is exact and one pass
the table needs 27ᵏ rows for k characters of context (19,683 for 3), most never seen
the net keeps the same loss, backward and update and only changes how logits are computed, so it grows into an MLP and a transformer

compare.q: micrograd's big ideas are about one scalar expression and its gradients; this course's are about a model of data. What does this course add on top of the micrograd loop, and which micrograd idea does it rely on without re-teaching?
answer: new: a dataset of (xs, ys) pairs, a probability model, and the average NLL instead of squared error
new: the parameters are one 27×27 tensor and the loss is vectorised over 228,146 examples
relied on: forward, zero the grads, backward, update; W.grad = None is micrograd's zero_grad
relied on: backprop fills W.grad exactly as micrograd's backward() did, just on tensors

compare.q: Both courses train with the same four-line loop. Which design choices differ (loss, learning rate, what the parameters are), and what caused each difference?
answer: loss: squared error on 4 numeric targets vs average NLL over 27 classes, because the output here is a probability distribution
learning rate: 0.1 vs 50, because this loss is an average over 228,146 examples and the model is one linear layer
parameters: 41 scalars in a Python MLP vs one 27×27 tensor whose optimum is known in advance (log N)

compare.q: The toolkit introduced softmax and cross-entropy as formulas. How does this course change what they mean, and where would the toolkit view alone leave you stuck?
answer: here softmax is exp-then-normalise of log-counts, the same step as dividing a row of N by its total
cross-entropy here is the average NLL from the counting route, so its value can be checked against 2.4540 and 3.2958
the formula alone doesn't tell you what a good or bad value is, or that a zero probability makes it infinite

predict.q: You start the neural bigram with W = torch.zeros((27, 27)) instead of random numbers, and train on all words with lr 50 and no regularisation. Commit first: what is the loss at step 0, and after 100 steps is it above or below the random start's 2.4729?
predict.answer: 3.2958 at step 0, exactly log 27: every logit is 0, every count is 1, every row is uniform. After 100 steps it is 2.4705, slightly below the random start's 2.4729 (computed), because it starts much closer (3.2958 vs 3.7590) with nothing confidently wrong to undo. Both still sit above counting's 2.4540. Start from W = log(N+1) instead and step 0 is already 2.4546.

apply.task: Build the whole course in one script, both routes. Count N from names.txt and score it (unsmoothed and with N + 1). Then build xs, ys over all words, train W with lr 50 for 100 steps and no regularisation, and print the loss at steps 0 and 99. Finally, sample 5 names from each model with the same seed and compare.
apply.done: Counting prints 2.4540 (2.4546 with N + 1); the net prints 3.7590 at step 0 and 2.4729 at step 99. With seed 2147483647 on torch 2.14 the net samples 'cexze.', 'momasurailezityha.', 'konimittain.', 'llayn.', 'ka.' (computed), and the smoothed counts give the same names except the second, 'momasurailezitynn.'.
apply.hint: Score the counting model with the same vectorised line the net uses: -P[xs, ys].log().mean().
